groups.root_cause: Setup does not reload or restart an already-healthy daemon after writing new configuration, so the daemon keeps running on its old settings.
Smoke checks run against a hardcoded set of built-in providers instead of the providers actually configured and available.
Setup saves newly selected repositories without first checking that they can be accessed.
Interactive initialization never asks for or saves the discreet-mode preference.
Doctor only probes providers that have an explicit health URL, so it never checks credentials for the others.
Init's already-configured check matches on the preset an entry uses, not its provider name, so an alias like work-claude counts as the native claude entry.
The shell quote/heredoc stripping removes command substitutions inside double-quoted strings and unquoted heredocs, even though the shell runs them, so the signal commands inside are never checked.
The JavaScript string stripping deletes template literal interpolations, which run as code, so signal calls inside them are never checked.
Inline eval detection only recognizes the space-separated option form and misses the standard equals form (--eval=...).
Wrapping the Codex CLI in an outer Seatbelt sandbox blocks the runtime it needs, including writes to its state directory, so tool-enabled agents can't initialize or start.
The sticky-implementer check treats any historical policy edit as invalidating, even for selections made after that edit, so later escalations are dropped.
The record of policy edits or invalidations is not persisted across daemon restarts, so a resumed run goes back to a saved implementer that a reset removed.
A stored operator override naming a model that no longer exists makes runtime-policy construction throw instead of skipping or tolerating it, and the CLI reset needs a running daemon.
A routing-change notification cancels every pending invocation across all roles instead of only those affected by the edited cell.
Validation failures put the raw zod issue JSON into the error message instead of a readable summary.
`eval policy` compares the proposed overlay with the effective policy, which includes operator overrides, instead of with the base overlay policy.
Resetting a cell does not check whether an override exists, so a no-op reset still writes history and broadcasts an SSE update.
The GUIDE says provider cards appear only on the Providers page, which doesn't match the Models page, which still renders them.
Persisted utilization warnings aren't cleared or suppressed when a provider switches to unlimited quota.
Config export always serializes the default quota = "windows" field, which older releases reject as an unknown field.
The output schema for the MCP providers tool doesn't include the new quota field, so it gets stripped from responses.
After escalation, the engine drops the exclusion for the exhausted implementer, so when the next implementer becomes unavailable, routing falls back to the exhausted one.
Environment-blocked verify retries do not keep the blocked verifier excluded, so the pinned chain picks the same verifier again instead of the available alternative.
The pinned-verify independence warning always names the implementer, even when the excluded model was a previous verifier or a finder.
In panel review mode, a single-entry review chain lets the finders run but leaves no allowed verifier once a finding is raised, so the run stops at needs_human after the finders have been paid for.
Pinned-chain handling throws away a decision model's low-confidence last-resort result instead of accepting it the way policy selection does.
Chain-mode routing ignores vendor independence as a tie-break between `|` alternatives, so it can pick the implementer's vendor and then wrongly log that no other vendor was available.
The audit's list of exempt inert media extensions leaves out requested types such as PDF and MP4, so these files need a binary allowance.
The PNG inspector treats ordinary ancillary metadata chunks, such as title or author text, as disqualifying and drops the exemption.
The media gate scans raw sample bytes for executable signatures such as MZ, so ordinary media data that happens to contain them is flagged.
The media gate adds an unrequested size cutoff based on decoded or header-declared size, which blocks valid large images and audio.
Executable/archive signatures such as MZ or ustar are matched anywhere in the content instead of only at the proper offset, so ordinary bytes get flagged as binary or executable.
The PNG validation is too strict about metadata chunks, so a valid image with an ordinary comment loses its exemption.
The audit's list of inert-media extensions leaves out the requested PDF, font and audio types.
Binary classification in repos.ts counts the executable file mode as binary content, so readable shell scripts need a binary allowance.
Classification reads the whole blob instead of a bounded sample, so large text files hit the output-size limit.

The legacy-worktree path is registered too late (after the needs_human throw and after preparation reuse), so resumed delivery and interrupted-preparation runs use the checkout before it is registered.
The regression tests only cover a resume in the loop phase and miss the draft-delivery restart path.
The migration decides which worktrees are legacy using a hard-coded timestamp cutoff. That cutoff does not match when each installation actually upgraded, and the test fixtures hide the gap.
The migration only treats a run as eligible if baseline-check evidence exists, but a run interrupted during prepare may never have emitted that evidence.
Worktree registration in the engine only accepts checkouts that come from the bare cache, so it rejects legacy checkouts that belong to the original local source repository.
On resume, the new headSha Git probe runs before the needsHuman check, so a Git error replaces the human-review status of runs that are already waiting for review.
An error while inspecting one PR's CI aborts the whole repository poll loop instead of being caught for that PR alone.
The main-red branch returns early, before job logs are fetched, so the ledger signature uses a generic conclusion instead of the real error and runner image.
Job URL validation compares the repository name case-sensitively against the operator-configured spelling.
Rerun resolution doesn't treat a skipped conclusion as a terminal result, so the retry never resolves.
When the rerun POST response is lost, nothing is persisted that would let the poller reconcile the accepted rerun with its later result.
Rerun lookup searches only the newest workflow attempt instead of searching across all attempts for the rerun job.
Main-red notifications are deduplicated per failing check instead of per repository.
Suppressed PRs are only re-inspected when the PR itself changes, not when main goes back to green.
Cancelled matrix legs are treated as rerunnable failures and recorded as flakes, even though fail-fast cancelled them and they never failed.
The rerun cap is used up before the rerun request succeeds, and GitHub's refusal for an in-progress workflow is mishandled as an access error instead of being deferred.
An unreleased new table is altered by a second migration in the same change instead of being defined once.
Rerun reconciliation depends on the single page of 100 GraphQL check contexts, so retried jobs past that page are never seen.
The poller emits failure notifications for closed tracked PRs without running them through the CI classifier.
The feed excerpt is taken from the start of the job log instead of the area around the failure.
The new `[github] ci_reruns` config switch and its enabled default are missing from GUIDE.md.
The signature extractor picks the first log line containing 'fail' or 'error', which is often an echoed input rather than the real failure.
Main-red state is cleared while main's newest commit still has pending checks, instead of being kept until the checks reach a final green result.
A definitively rejected rerun request is never resolved, so the classification stays pending forever and never yields a fix result.
A CI inspection error on one PR stops the whole repository poll loop, so later PRs are never processed.
Persisted CI pauses skip the GraphQL-change guard, so every unchanged poll repeats REST inspection of each paused PR.
Repository URLs are compared case-sensitively, so valid jobs whose capitalization differs from the registered URL are rejected.
Failures classified as main-red are never written to the flake ledger.
Only the latest workflow attempt is examined, so a later sibling-job rerun hides the attempt the factory started.
Completed reruns with skipped or neutral conclusions are not treated as terminal, so they never resolve.
Main's legacy commit statuses are only checked when the PR also has legacy statuses, so a red main is missed.
Rerunning a job also reruns its downstream dependent security jobs, which ignores the security-test exclusion.
The decision to rerun a whole job doesn't check whether the job contains security-test steps, so those steps get rerun.
Timeout detection only recognizes Bun and Playwright diagnostics, so other test-runner timeouts are not treated as transient.
The feed excerpt takes the first 2000 characters of the raw log, which is runner-setup boilerplate rather than the failure context.
The failure signature uses the first line loosely matching error/fail, so distinct failures collide on the same signature.
The change is far larger than the requested source budget, including a redundant second migration for the same new table.
When GitHub refuses a rerun request (for example, due to rate limiting), the saved rerun claim is never released or resolved, so it stays pending through cooldowns and restarts.
The security-failure heading patterns in the retry exclusion are too narrow, so security-test failures from some runners (Playwright, Go) are missed and the jobs get rerun.
The timeout regex misses common runner timeout diagnostics, such as Node test-runner messages and indented, untimestamped Playwright lines, so transient timeouts are not rerun.
An error while inspecting one PR's CI aborts the whole poll, so later PRs' observations are lost.
The main-red pause path returns before the PR failure is written to the ledger.
The API URL repository check compares owner and repo names case-sensitively.
Reconciliation looks only at the newest workflow attempt, which may be a partial rerun that does not include the tracked job.
Pending reruns are reconciled only when the paginated, capped check observation changes, so reruns outside the first 100 checks are never resolved.
While main is red or a rerun is pending, the full REST inspection runs again on every poll even when the GraphQL observation is unchanged.
Whenever observePrHead refuses, for example during a push or with a stuck pushing marker, the whole observation is discarded.
A failed job in lagging check data is still classified as needing a fix even after its rerun was confirmed passing.
Main-red alerts are deduplicated per check rather than per repository.
The main-branch status lookup only queries the context types the PR uses, so main failures reported through other types are missed.
CI failures observed after a PR has closed skip the classification path.
Rerun reconciliation treats only success and failure as terminal, so skipped or neutral conclusions stay pending.
The feed excerpt is taken from the start of the job log instead of around the failure.
The failure signature is taken from the first line containing 'error', which can be setup noise rather than the actual failure.
Untrusted log text is quoted with an ad-hoc '> ' prefix instead of the project's existing quoting helper.
A second migration alters a table that was created by another migration in the same unshipped change.
The security name regex has no word boundaries, so it matches unrelated substrings such as 'disaster'.
Jobs cancelled by fail-fast are treated as transient, then rerun and recorded as flakes.
The cache of rejected models is keyed so that it outlives a fix to the backend name, or deleting and recreating the model, for up to 24 hours.
The PATCH update logic gives no way to unset default effort, so the field can't be cleared.
Probe responses that arrive after a provider is disabled and re-enabled are not checked against the current generation, so an older response can overwrite newer discovery results.
At boot, loading runtime catalog entries throws a fatal error when an entry's name collides with a config model or its provider no longer exists, instead of skipping or reconciling the entry.
Smoke filters out providers that are disabled or missing without logging a skip or failing, so their checks silently disappear.
Smoke opens the live production database and applies the checkout's unshipped migrations before the release is accepted.
The test client decodes the :id parameter itself, so the tests never check that the server decodes encoded model names.
The escaped-process fixture depends on the child starting before the timeout fires, so a slow start triggers a retry and the test fails.
Eval eligibility doesn't apply the served-model guard, so models that discovery has confirmed are absent still get run.
When a backend is replaced or its catalog entry is deleted and recreated, the old model rejection block is not cleared, so the new backend inherits it.
The PATCH handler cannot unset a model's configured default effort, so the model can't fall back to the server default.
Deleting a runtime model doesn't check whether the file-backed routing policy still references it, so the next startup fails policy validation.
Provider probe responses aren't sequenced, so an older health response that arrives late overwrites newer discovery results.
Loading the persisted runtime catalog at startup throws when an entry clashes with a config model of the same name or its provider no longer exists, instead of handling that entry gracefully.
The cleanup test assumes only the first attempt's process IDs exist, but smoke retries can start before the test sees readiness and add a second pair.
The eval runner calls catalog models without the served-model availability guard, so models discovery marks unavailable still get invoked.
Queued chat requests keep the model they picked before waiting and don't check it again after acquiring the slot, so they can call a backend discovery has since removed.
The smoke check now reads runtime provider state and silently drops checks for disabled providers, without reporting them as skipped.
The retry picker has no error handling for a failed routing load, so it stays in the loading state with submission disabled.
When default effort is cleared, the PATCH payload leaves the field out instead of sending an explicit clear, so the old value stays stored.
Catalog history is kept only in component-local state, not loaded from the server, so it is lost when Setup unmounts and never shows changes made by other clients.
An out-of-scope Playwright dependency was added along with a postinstall script that downloads Chromium on every install.
Every provider SSE event triggers a full page refetch with one preview request per cell, with no debouncing and no cancellation of overlapping batches.
The retry panel shows role-specific validation errors in two separate alert regions, so the same error appears twice.

The final cleanup in the finally block can throw, and that error replaces the recoverable cleanup error, so the whole run fails instead of moving on to another round. This happens at a different site from G3's discard-changes path and needs its own fix.
On Darwin, process ownership is decided by matching working directory and start time, so unrelated orphaned processes in the same cwd get claimed and killed.
The gate-timeout rerun path in the engine calls cleanup without the retry and recovery handling used on other paths, so a temporary cleanup failure aborts the whole run.
Darwin descendant discovery depends on an inherited environment marker, so a descendant that replaces its environment is no longer found and keeps running after cleanup reports success.

Cleanup treats any orphaned process whose cwd is inside the checkout as the invocation's own, so it kills unrelated jobs that just happen to run there. This is a different over-claiming heuristic from G2's recycled PID group and session IDs.

Once the launcher exits, the only way cleanup finds detached descendants is by matching their cwd or inherited environment. A child that runs from another directory or replaces its environment is never found, so it survives while cleanup still reports success.
On Darwin, processes are treated as owned by the invocation if they share its working directory and started after it, so unrelated processes get killed.

Descendant discovery depends on inherited environment markers and working-directory heuristics, so helpers with a replaced environment are missed even when they share the process group. Shutdown is then reported as complete while they are still alive.
The rerun path after a gate timeout calls cleanup without the retry/recovery handling used elsewhere, so one cleanup failure ends the run.
Replacing HOME in the reader environment drops the default Rust toolchain location (~/.cargo, ~/.rustup), so the confined verifier can't find the installed compiler.
The loopback network rule lets confined commands bind any local port instead of only ephemeral ports, so they can reserve ports other services need.
The criterion parser only partly parses the instruction text. It pulls out one test command and treats that as proof of the whole criterion, so steps or filenames it drops are never checked.
Gate evidence counts a successful exit code as proof of the targeted tests without positive evidence that those exact tests ran.

Commit provenance is recorded without checking that the tested working-tree bytes match the commit, so a setup step that changed the code can produce passing results that get credited to the original commit.
On resume, cached gate results are skipped but their evidence is rejected because the stage was never marked successful, so the criterion stays blocked forever.
Gate-evidence substitution depends on detecting free-text claims in the model's wording, so passing observations that merely mention gates get misclassified and downgraded to environment blocks.
The loopback workaround rejects gate evidence whenever any test was skipped, rather than checking only whether the required test was skipped.
Verification matches commands exactly and ignores the recorded file coverage, so Bun's suffix-based filename filter can run a different file and the requested test still gets marked verified.
The engine treats an unchanged HEAD as proof that gates tested the committed tree, even though setup commands or earlier checks can change the working tree and those changes are later discarded.
Targeted Bun evidence is accepted because the command matches exactly, without checking recorded coverage that the requested test file actually ran.
Verification rejects the whole gate when any test is skipped, even an unrelated one, instead of only checking the tests tied to the criterion.
Test-coverage parsing treats output the candidate controls as authoritative, so a fabricated passing line counts as real coverage.

MCP status checks old landing blockers before closed-PR observations, so a closed PR still gets fix-and-requeue advice.
The land list endpoint now rejects an empty run query parameter instead of treating it as no filter.
MCP verdict handling hardcodes the reviewer as "human" instead of attributing the verdict to the MCP agent.
The Codex skill's digest command passes the consumer name 'claude' instead of a Codex-specific consumer.
MCP status ignores the run's confirmed-merged flag, so it still tells agents to review a PR that has already merged.
The digest's awaiting-review filter doesn't exclude runs that have an active changes round, so it asks for a review before that work is finished.
The digest's acknowledgment filtering drops PRs whose approval was invalidated by a new push, even when they have unread CI results.
The digest doesn't check the confirmed-merged flag before showing blocked-land alerts, so the old alert keeps appearing after an operator merges the PR.
The session-start digest fetches run details and landing info one at a time across the whole unacked feed, instead of limiting or batching those lookups.
The quoting helper doesn't escape bidi-override or zero-width characters in untrusted PR text.
Digest lines have no length cap, so a long question or title is inserted into the agent's context in full.
When the saved PR snapshot has no headRefOid, status falls back to an old failed review round instead of saying the current head is unknown.
getRunDetail queries the latest approval row twice instead of reusing the first result.
MCP review verdicts hardcode the reviewer as "human" instead of recording the agent's identity.

When the private-strings policy fails to load, limitless_status falls back to a response that drops the state and nextAction fields.
Status checks for a historical landing block before checking closed or resolved states, so a stale block wins over the current state.
The digest treats a missing PR head snapshot as a mismatch with the approval, so an approved PR shows up again as awaiting review.
Digest lines are not truncated, so untrusted run text of any length gets injected into agent context.
A new test assertion is not formatted, which fails the required format check.
In status derivation, an approval takes priority over an active review or repair round and hides the ongoing work.
The Codex skill documentation tells Codex to run the digest command with the 'claude' feed consumer instead of its own.
getRunDetail runs the latest-approval query twice when one query would do.

The Codex skill file tells Codex to use the Claude consumer name, so it reads Claude's cursor instead of its own.
The MCP review and land handlers pass the backend's mutation result through without checking it against a schema.

Out-of-order tool completions overwrite the previous-result baseline, so stale output from an older call replaces a newer call's baseline.
The loop detector aborts on the threshold call before that call's result can show progress.
While the invocation is running, tool calls that never get a result are left out of the repetition count, so repeated unresolved calls go on with no limit.
One call that never returns blocks the in-order processing at line 206, so later identical calls that did complete are never counted as a loop.
The bounded window at line 180 can drop unresolved calls before they are counted, so the session-end check misses the loop too.
A parallel call that completes out of order is judged repetitive using predecessor calls that haven't resolved yet, so the agent can be stopped before those calls show progress.
Loop detection now runs only when a call's result arrives, so a repeated call that never resolves is never checked and the agent is not stopped.
When a call is evicted from the window, the previous result hash is discarded too, so a later change in output is not recognised as progress and the agent is stopped one repetition early.
The strict eval GateResultSchema doesn't allow the newly added optional failures/excerpt field.
Any line starting with 'not ok ' is treated as a TAP failure boundary without checking it is a real TAP result line, so log output can fill all the failure slots.

Implementer feedback truncation keeps the start of each excerpt and drops the end, so the assertion error, diff and (fail) line are lost first.

The land log character budget at queue.ts:318 is too small when excerpts are present: it shrinks the raw tail to 1,000 characters and is below the excerpt cap, so excerpts get clipped and noted twice.
Failure excerpts are clipped before credential redaction runs, so credentials stay in excerpts and fragments cut by clipping can't be removed by literal redaction afterwards.
Runtime catalog rows that are now redundant with a built-in can't be removed, because remove rejects ids that resolve to read-only built-ins and nothing prunes them automatically.
Collision tolerance is keyed to the literal id claude/haiku-5.5 instead of applying to any built-in that shadows a runtime entry.
When the built-in replaces the runtime model, saved operator routing choices aren't checked against the built-in's supported efforts, so an effort it doesn't support makes startup fail.
The pin test hard-codes the decision date and eval ids instead of reading them from overrides.json.
The frozen routing identity test removes Haiku 5.5 from every role before comparing, so the widened-chain changes it causes are never checked.
The triage.default reason in overrides.json was replaced rather than extended, so the earlier decision history was lost.
Eval resume rejects the whole request when the saved state mentions a retired model, when it should drop or skip that model and keep going with the supported targets and fallbacks.
Loading persisted operator routing overrides at startup fails hard on retired IDs instead of filtering them out, so the daemon cannot start.
Parsing the SSH destination in local management does not handle bare IPv6 addresses, so it throws before SSH is ever contacted.
The configured provider is found by matching the SSH destination string against the provider's HTTP origin, which fails when an alias and an IP refer to the same host.
The anchor in the OPERATIONS.md link to the GUIDE's LAN provider example points to the wrong section.
OPERATIONS.md still gives the old llama-server binary location, which no longer matches the generated unit's new default path.
Catalog additions that bring back a missing model are accepted without checking that model's saved routing and preference references against its new settings, so the daemon fails at its next startup.
The filtered operator routing is built once at startup and is not rebuilt when the catalog changes, so a restored model is not used for routing until the daemon restarts.
Building the URL for the SSH destination in src/cli/local.ts does not put brackets around IPv6 addresses, so it throws before any management command runs.

Provider matching in src/cli/local.ts does not account for providers reached through an SSH tunnel, so the health probe goes to the wrong endpoint without the API key and the provider's enablement is never updated.
The resume/retry check rejects a whole historical eval if any saved model is retired, when it should skip the retired model and continue with the available ones.

Startup validation of stored prefer and REMOVED_MODELS cells was weakened to treat any unknown value as a retired model, so a misplaced model ID gets a misleading error and the fail-loud tests were removed.
Catalog additions that bring back a model referenced by saved routing rules are not checked against those rules, so a mismatch in supported settings only fails at the next daemon startup.
Resolving saved references rejects the whole resume or retry when any referenced model is retired, instead of skipping retired entries and using the available targets or fallbacks.
The remote-host validation in local management is too strict and rejects IPv6 addresses before SSH is invoked.
The remote host value is passed to SSH without blocking option-like values (such as a leading dash), so SSH treats it as an option and status can falsely report the service as active.

Providers are linked to the remote host only by an exact match on http://<remote_host>:8080, so SSH aliases or other ports break enabling/disabling the provider and the health check, which also omits the API key.
No end-to-end test covers reading the [local].remote_* keys from config.toml into local management.
Credential redaction runs only after the process runner has already truncated raw output, so a secret that crosses the truncation boundary gets cut and escapes redaction.
Redaction checks one line at a time, so it never matches a credential that spans two lines, and the full secret reappears when the failure excerpt rebuilds the lines.
The verify-prompt redaction tests make assertions that pass whether or not redaction happens, so they can't catch a regression.
The baseline cache key or version wasn't changed when redaction was added, so unredacted results cached before the upgrade are still reused and copied into new artifacts.
Failure excerpts are built from per-line callbacks, so pieces of a multiline credential are never matched and redacted.
Output is truncated before sanitization, so a cut inside an ANSI sequence leaves part of the credential unredacted.
Restoring run state runs redaction and sanitization over execution fields such as phase and command snapshot, which corrupts the trusted state.
Coverage paths are redacted before alias canonicalization, so a resolved filename containing a credential is returned without redaction.
The HTTP layer applies a sanitizing rewrite to every response, including artifact downloads, which changes the stored diagnostic content.
Prompt input redaction strips terminal escape sequences from the inline patch, so the patch under review no longer matches the real change.
The tail-cut overlap is too small to cover the longest supported JSON-escaped credential variants, so a cut-through credential partly survives redaction.
Excerpt line framing drops content such as blank lines, so multiline credentials no longer match before the excerpt is stored.
Retained failure-excerpt lines have no byte limit, so very long diagnostic lines are kept without bound.
Separately registered credential fragments are redacted before the full multiline credential, which stops the full credential from matching.
The privacy filter treats any text containing the literal "[redacted]" as private and withholds the whole thing, even when it holds no secret.
redactGateData is applied to whole API, prompt, report and state payloads, not just gate output, so it changes and saves over data that is not gate output.
The artifact endpoint parses JSON artifacts and serializes them again in compact form instead of serving the stored file bytes as they are.
Terminal formatting is stripped only after the runner has already framed and tail-cut the output, so credential fragments split by escape sequences slip past redaction.
The carry is redacted as soon as the shorter credential matches, so the sensitive suffix of a longer registered credential that shares its prefix gets emitted in a later chunk.
The failure-excerpt path never gets ANSI-normalized, multiline-aware redaction, so a formatted multiline credential comes back whole in the excerpt.
The privacy filter treats the literal "[redacted]" marker as sensitive and withholds the entire text instead of passing the already-redacted content through.
The HTTP/SSE layer runs gate-data redaction on every response object, which rewrites non-gate payloads and adds confinement metadata to them.
The artifact endpoint parses and sanitizes stored artifacts instead of serving the stored bytes unchanged, which alters JSON formatting and strips escape bytes from non-gate artifacts like patches.
Prompt construction runs gate-output sanitization over every input, including the patch under review, which removes literal escape bytes from the source changes.
The new stdoutTruncated/stderrTruncated fields are added to the process result but nothing reads them.
confinementError is now always written and saved output is VT-normalized, so an older release reading results after a rollback can mistake the normalized text for a real confinement failure.
Moving the cut point across dense overlapping credential matches removes the bound on the streaming carry buffer, so it can grow without limit.
Restoring run state applies credential redaction to the executable gate configuration, and checkpoints then save the altered command.
Gate output is redacted before the sandbox startup marker is detected, so a credential that occurs inside the marker breaks startup detection.
Gate-specific output normalization (adding a confinement verdict and stripping escapes) is applied to every object and HTTP response, not only to gate results.
The output privacy filter treats any text containing the "[redacted]" marker as sensitive and withholds the whole field.
stdout and stderr are redacted separately and then joined, so a credential split across the two streams is rebuilt in the stored tail.
The deployment path in the CLI service runs gates without first registering configured credentials in the redaction registry.
New stdoutTruncated/stderrTruncated result fields were added that no production code reads.

Changing the test command string in .limitless.toml means it no longer matches the command the factory recorded, so the factory can't use its existing passing test run as evidence for verification. G2 is a different problem: the gate environment drops the worker override.
Thinking events are clipped to 2,000 characters before the owner diagnostic copy is captured, so the owner copy loses the rest of the original text.
Raw owner diagnostics stay in the shared database with no protection that holds up after a rollback, so agents started by an older release can read them.
The owner_diagnostics primary key lacks AUTOINCREMENT, so IDs freed by deletion can be reused and fall behind cursors that follow logs.
Preview or build code can reach the owner-only diagnostics table through the store, and the factory copies its output into public stage summaries.
The cached-evidence check doesn't handle a crash between saving passing gate results and marking the gate stage complete, so unchanged work gets wrongly sent for human intervention.
The amended-commit guard runs only after the initial pull-request lookup, so an earlier failure falls through to the draft fallback, which pushes the stale verified commit.
The pending-merge exception checks only the merge's parents and not its tree or content, so an amended merge with unreviewed file changes is accepted and published.
Compact run inspection output includes the full dependency array with no limit, so responses can grow past their size budgets.
The MCP proxy forwards the repo filter to the daemon but never checks that it was applied, so older daemons return unfiltered runs from other repositories.
